stops.name: Oberweissbach, the parsonage of the Thuringian Forest
stops.campa: In the high forest village of Oberweissbach, in the little principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, Friedrich Wilhelm August Fröbel is born on 21 April 1782, sixth child of the pastor Johann Jacob Fröbel. The parsonage stands under the great church; the father tends five thousand souls scattered over six villages and has little left for the newest one under his roof. The forest breathes around the village. The child who will one day plant gardens for children opens his eyes among firs.
stops.quote: I was born at Oberweissbach, a village in the Thuringian Forest, in the small principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, on the 21st April, 1782. My father was the principal clergyman, or pastor, there.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827), tr. Michaelis & Moore

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the mother's death
stops.campa: Nine months she nurses him; then Jacobine Eleonore Fröbel, born Hoffmann, fails and dies before her son's first spring. The wound is cut that the whole pedagogy will answer: a lifetime spent restoring to all children the mother-arms he never had. Fröbel himself will name this death the deciding event of his outward life. The infant is handed to servants; the father, buried in his parish and in the building of a new church, withdraws. In the motherless parsonage the seed of the Mutter- und Koselieder is laid.
stops.quote: Soon after my birth my mother's health began to fail, and after nursing me nine months she died. This loss, a hard blow to me, influenced the whole environment and development of my being: I consider that my mother's death decided more or less the external circumstances of my whole life.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the walled yard and the strip of sky
stops.campa: A stepmother enters the house and coldness with her; the boy is forbidden the street and confined to the walled yard between church and outbuildings. His whole horizon is the big church in front, the sloping field behind, and above him the clear hill-country sky. Deprived of distance, he learns nearness: the plants of the narrow garden become his first companions, and helping his father at gardening his first office. The sky seen from a walled garden: the child will spend a life giving that sky to other children.
stops.quote: For a long time I remained thus deprived of any distant view: but above me I saw the sky, clear and bright as we so often find it in the hill country; and around me I felt the pure fresh breeze stirring.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the hazel buds open the temple
stops.campa: The boy, troubled beyond his years by the sermons' talk of the flesh, is shown by his eldest brother the purple threads of the hazel buds and told that the flowers too are wedded, that sex runs quietly through all creation. The oppression lifts at once. Humanity and nature, soul-life and flower-life, knit together in him in that instant and never again come apart. He receives here, at nine years old, the clue of Ariadne he will follow through the labyrinth: the plant as the mirror of the human being.
stops.quote: I can still see my hazel buds, like angels, opening for me the great God's temple of Nature.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Stadtilm, the uncle's rescue
stops.campa: Superintendent Hoffmann, the dead mother's gentle brother, visits the parsonage, sees what the household is doing to the boy, and writes asking for him entirely. Towards the end of 1792 Friedrich comes to Stadtilm in the wide valley of the Ilm. Where the father's house held severity, mistrust and walls, the uncle's holds mildness, trust and liberty: forty schoolfellows, gardens open to him, the whole valley his playground. He drinks life in long draughts and gains freedom of soul and strength of body: the first proof, lived in his own skin, that kindness educates.
stops.quote: In my father's house severity reigned supreme; here, on the contrary, mildness and kindness held sway. There I encountered mistrust; here I was trusted. There I was under restraint; here I had liberty.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Neuhaus am Rennweg, apprentice to the forester
stops.campa: On Midsummer Day 1797, fifteen and a half years old, Fröbel is bound apprentice to a forester and land-surveyor two days' journey from home. The master, busy with timber-floating, leaves the boy alone in the forest house for weeks, and the forest itself takes over the teaching. He maps the neighbourhood, borrows botany books from a doctor in the little town, collects and dries plants with the greatest care, and walks home from the strolling players' theatre under the stars, fixing moral resolutions in his mind. His church religion quietly becomes a religion of the woods.
stops.quote: My religious church life now changed to a religious communion with Nature, and in the last half-year I lived entirely amongst and with my plants, which drew me towards them with fascination.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Jena, the university of the plant
stops.campa: Carrying money to his student brother in Jena, the seventeen-year-old sees the university city in its high noon, the Jena of Fichte and Schelling, of the young Romantics, and refuses to leave. A small maternal inheritance is unlocked; he matriculates. He hears mathematics, mineralogy, botany, natural history, forest-culture, chemistry, house-building; the air itself carries the doctrine that nature is one living whole. What the forest taught him wordlessly, Jena begins to say aloud: one law unfolds through stone, plant and man.

stops.name: Jena, the botanical garden: the plant unfolding
stops.campa: In Batsch's lecture-room and the ducal botanical garden Fröbel watches the plant do openly what the child does in secret: unfold from within, by inner law, needing not to be made but only tended. The lectures on natural history give him for the first time the image of interconnection: each organism a member of one developing whole. Here the master-metaphor of his life takes root: the educator as gardener, the school as garden, the child as a growing plant whose law must be obeyed, not overridden. The word Kindergarten lies forty years ahead, already germinating.
stops.quote: An intimate communion with Nature for more than thirty years... has taught me that plants, especially trees, are a mirror, or rather a symbol, of human life in its highest spiritual relations.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Jena, nine weeks in the university prison
stops.campa: Thirty thalers owed to an eating-house keeper, a father who refuses to pay, a stepmother who inflames him, a trustee who hides behind the letter of the law; and the student is locked nine weeks in the Karzer of Jena. He does not waste the cell: he grinds at Latin grammar, reads Winckelmann's letters, and keeps his inner life alight. Freedom comes only when he formally renounces, before the university board, all claim on his father's inheritance. He walks out disinherited and unbowed: the first of many times the world will make him pay for being Fröbel.
stops.quote: I served as scapegoat to the caprices of the obstinate couple, and languished as such nine weeks long in the university prison at Jena.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the father's death
stops.campa: Called home from his first small forestry post, Fröbel keeps the last months of watch at the bedside of the stern pastor who never understood him. In 1802 Johann Jacob Fröbel dies, and the parsonage that was never a home closes behind the son forever. Twenty years old, orphaned twice over, he is now wholly unhoused, and therefore wholly free. The wander-years begin: surveyor, actuary, secretary, a man carrying an unnamed calling from post to post like sealed orders he has not yet been permitted to open.

stops.name: Bamberg, land-surveyor in the secularised bishopric
stops.campa: Early in the spring of 1803 he goes to Bamberg, guessing rightly that the political redrawing of the old episcopal lands will need surveyors. He is taken on at once, maps the town and its district, and holds for a time a government clerkship. The work is measurement: chains, angles, the reduction of living land to line and number. It teaches him exactness while starving his soul. In the evenings he reads Novalis and asks the question that will not be quiet: what is a man for? The compass in his hand keeps pointing somewhere the maps do not show.

stops.name: Gross-Milchow, private secretary in Mecklenburg
stops.campa: The wander-years carry him far north, to the flat raw country of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, as private secretary on the estate of Gross-Milchow. Accounts, letters, the administration of another man's land: the outer life orderly, the inner life burning. Here he resolves at last to make something of himself by a settled profession, and fixes on architecture: the building of forms by law. He does not yet know that the resolve is a cipher, and that the building he is being sent to raise is made of children. From Gross-Milchow the road runs to Frankfurt.
